inputs.question: What is the workload?
inputs.answer: pd.to_datetime on a list of daily date strings 1900-2000 with format containing %z, plus one string with a different offset

known: Workload parses one daily date string per day from 1900 to 2000 with %z, plus one string with +02:00 offset (workload.py:6-10)
unknown: Relative cost of each stage; no profile supplied
assumed: Per-element Timestamp construction and tz_localize cost dominates a vectorised conversion
derived: Element count is the number of days in 1900..2000 plus one, from workload.py:6-7

root_causes.description: Tz-aware results of format-based parsing are materialised one Python Timestamp at a time instead of by vectorised conversion per distinct offset
Per-row Python-level regex group handling and offset parsing in array_strptime without memoisation per distinct offset string

findings.problem: When array_strptime returns any timezone, every element is converted through a Python list comprehension that builds a Timestamp and calls tz_localize on it, followed by np.array and Index inference over the resulting object array.
findings.performance_principle: Bulk data should be transformed with batch operations over homogeneous groups, not by constructing one heavyweight object per element.

evidence.statement: Per-element Python loop: np.array([Timestamp(res).tz_localize(zone) for res, zone in zip(result, timezones)]).
With utc=True a second per-element loop runs tz_convert/tz_localize on each Timestamp.
Taken whenever any timezone is non-None, so all elements of the workload use this path.
Timezones come from pytz.FixedOffset(minutes), so distinct offsets are few (two in the workload) while elements are many. No runtime evidence supplied.

findings.conditions: Any to_datetime call with an explicit format containing %z or %Z over a large list or array; cost scales with length. The workload matches (one element per day over 1900-2000).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for a vectorised or grouped path for tz results in this function and in _array_strptime_with_fallback; none exists.
Mixed offsets cannot form a single tz-aware DatetimeIndex, so the output must be an object Index of Timestamps; some per-element object creation is inherent in that case.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: With mixed offsets (as in the workload, one odd row) the output must be an object Index of Timestamps, so some per-element creation is unavoidable; the saving is then only redundant intermediate work. Real share depends on a profile versus array_strptime.
findings.recommendation: Group by distinct tzinfo (few) and localize whole int64 blocks once per group; if all offsets are identical return a tz-aware DatetimeIndex directly (and for utc=True convert once). Materialise per-element Timestamps only for the genuinely mixed-offset object result, and avoid the redundant second pass.

alternatives.option: Group by unique tz and use vectorised tz_localize on slices
alternatives.why: Removes per-element object work in the common homogeneous case

alternatives.option: Have array_strptime return UTC-normalised int64 plus offsets and build Timestamps from that
alternatives.why: Larger change to the Cython return contract

findings.trade_offs: More branches (homogeneous vs mixed); must preserve existing return types for mixed offsets.

validation.metric: Wall time of the workload's to_datetime call; cProfile cumulative time of _return_parsed_timezone_results
validation.expectation: Direction: lower time, with this function's share shrinking; magnitude unmeasured.
validation.falsifier: A profile showing this function is a small fraction of total time.
validation.guard: Add an asv benchmark for to_datetime with a %z format on a large list.

commands.purpose: Profile where time is spent in the workload (to be run by the maintainer)

findings.problem: Each row builds a groupdict, loops over group keys with Python-object dict lookups, and re-parses the %z string via parse_timezone_directive (slicing, several int() calls, pytz.FixedOffset) although offset strings repeat heavily.
findings.performance_principle: Repeated work on a small set of distinct inputs should be done once per distinct value.

evidence.statement: groupdict and per-key dispatch run for every element.
parse_timezone_directive is called per row with no memo of already-parsed offset strings.
parse_timezone_directive does slicing, three int() conversions and a pytz.FixedOffset call.

findings.conditions: Large inputs with %z where offset strings repeat; the workload has two distinct offset strings across all rows.

counter_evidence.statement: Regex matching and groupdict are inherent to this strptime design and also run without %z; only the offset re-parse is avoidable.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: The per-row regex match and date construction likely dominate, and pytz.FixedOffset already caches tz objects, so a memo saves only the string parsing.
findings.recommendation: Memoise parse_timezone_directive results in a dict keyed by the raw offset string within one array_strptime call.

alternatives.option: Per-call dict memo of offset string to tzinfo

findings.trade_offs: A small dict per call; negligible.

validation.metric: Time of array_strptime on a list with repeated %z offsets
validation.expectation: Small improvement in direction only; not quantified.

considered_not_reported.observation: Regex cache lookup under a lock in array_strptime
evidence_checked: regex cache lookup under lock, once per call
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: O(1) per call, not per element
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: to_datetime is called in a tight loop with many small inputs
